actions.body: Intellectual curiosity has historically been a primary driver of scientific advancement, as evidenced by the proliferation of observational tools like the telescope. Modern machine learning research into developmental robotics suggests that these biological mechanisms of curiosity—intrinsic motivation and curiosity-driven learning—can be modeled as computational frameworks. By focusing on predictive world models and learning progress, artificial agents can begin to approximate autonomous problem formulation. This integration of history and computation forms the basis of the current inquiry into how artificial systems might independently identify research problems. Summary: Curiosity, whether in human history or robotic development, functions as an internal reward mechanism that allows an agent to prioritize exploration and knowledge acquisition, providing a theoretical foundation for autonomous, instruction-free research processes.
actions.lede: Connecting historical accounts of curiosity to modern machine learning frameworks for autonomous discovery.

Exponential growth of scientific literature and increasing domain specialization constrain researchers' capacity to synthesize knowledge across disciplines and develop unifying theories, motivating exploration of general-purpose AI systems for science. Here we show that a domain-agnostic, agentic AI Scientist system can independently navigate the scientific workflow -from hypothesis generation through data collection to manuscript preparation. The system autonomously designed and executed three psychological studies on visual working memory, mental rotation, and imagery vividness, executed online data collection with 288 participants, developed analysis pipelines through 8h+ continuous coding sessions, and produced completed manuscripts. The results demonstrate the capability of AI scientific discovery pipelines to conduct research with theoretical reasoning and methodological rigor comparable to experienced researchers, though with limitations in conceptual nuance and theoretical interpretation. This is a step toward embodied AI that can test hypotheses through real-world experiments, accelerating discovery by autonomously exploring regions of scientific space that human cognitive and resource constraints might otherwise leave unexplored. It raises important questions about the nature of scientific understanding and attribution of scientific credit.\", \"doi\": \"10.1002/advs.76675\", \"pmid\": \"42734488\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13573717\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.76675\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13573717\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13573717?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Transforming Molecular Science With Large Language Models: From Molecule Understanding to Autonomous Scientific Discovery.\", \"abstract\": \"Large language models (LLMs) are driving a paradigm shift in molecular science, transitioning from molecule understanding to autonomous scientific discovery. By learning from multimodal molecular representations through advanced training techniques, LLMs address traditional limitations in molecular research, including expert dependency and limited experimental scalability. We analyze strategies for cross-modal alignment and domain adaptation that enable LLMs to interpret complex molecular semantics. This deep semantic understanding translates into broad versatility across key downstream applications, encompassing retrieval tasks like molecule-text matching, prediction tasks like reaction outcome inference, and generative tasks including zero-shot molecule design. Crucially, we highlight how LLMs integrate with robotic platforms to establish closed-loop autonomous discovery systems, where AI agents automate hypothesis generation, experimental planning, and iterative validation. While these advances accelerate exploration of molecular space, persistent challenges remain in scaling experimental validation and bridging symbolic reasoning with physical experimentation. This review provides a comprehensive roadmap for leveraging LLMs to redefine scientific discovery in molecular science.\", \"doi\": \"10.1002/asia.70837\", \"pmid\": \"42289772\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13355129\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1002/asia.70837\"}, {\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availabilityCode\": \"F\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13355129\"}, {\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availabilityCode\": \"F\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13355129?pdf=render\"}, {\"availability\": \"Free\", \"availabilityCode\": \"F\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.1002/asia.70837\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"AI agents in cancer imaging: Concepts, advances, and clinical perspectives.\", \"abstract\": \"Medical imaging serves as a critical source of evidence for cancer diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up. However, most existing medical imaging artificial intelligence (AI) systems still operate on predefined tasks and inputs, limiting their ability to address the evolving needs of clinical practice and research. AI agents use foundation models as central engines for reasoning and orchestration. They organize analytical processes according to task objectives, invoke external tools and data resources, and adapt subsequent actions based on intermediate results. They may therefore facilitate a shift in cancer imaging AI from isolated model applications toward continuous workflow support. This review outlines the fundamental principles, system components, and evaluation approaches for AI agents from a cancer imaging perspective and summarizes representative advances in image interpretation, clinical decision support, and research workflows. article.body:
Imagine you are building a puzzle, but instead of just placing pieces, you also constantly check to see if the picture on the box matches the one you are building. As an analogy, we are looking at how computer workers examine how artificial systems monitor their own choices during complex tasks. [1, 2, 3]

The group is investigating metareasoning. This term means thinking about thinking. It describes how a system manages its limited mental resources, deciding when to stop planning and start doing. Recent work shows this process is crucial for efficiency. [1]

We are also learning about the limits of this process. Some recorded readings suggest that relying on a system to correct its own mistakes without outside help is fundamentally limited. These systems often struggle to identify the foundational assumptions behind their errors. [2, 8]

To tackle this, some members are looking at philosophy, specifically how science progresses by treating ideas like theories that must be tested and potentially proven wrong, rather than just accepted. This Popperian approach suggests that systems might need to be designed to seek out their own failures. [5, 6]

Other members are exploring how systems might choose problems on their own. This involves curiosity-driven learning, where a system explores because it finds something interesting rather than just following a set path. This shifts the role of the machine from a passive follower to an active investigator. [3, 9, 10, 12]

When multiple agents work together, they face coordination challenges. We are seeing how structured communication helps them align their actions. These frameworks help different systems manage information exchange effectively, improving their joint performance. [11]

Maintaining a steady history is also difficult. How does an agent keep track of who it is and what it decided across different turns? Some models are now using persistent self-models to manage their operational history, which helps maintain accountability. [4]

We are also tracking how systems develop stable preferences. It seems these preferences are often path-dependent, meaning the history of what a system experienced shapes what it wants now, rather than being an absolute truth. [7]

If an intelligent system cannot reliably correct its own foundational logic, can we build external guardrails that verify its work without slowing it down so much that it becomes useless? [1, 2, 8]

Summary

We study how computers think about their own reasoning. We find that fixing mistakes internally is difficult for these systems. They often need help from outside to verify their work. Some researchers are testing if systems can pick their own problems to solve. Others are looking at how they work together in groups. We do not know yet if systems can truly question their own starting rules. We continue to watch the Console for new research.
article.lede: We continue our look at how artificial systems manage their internal thinking, shifting focus from fixed rules to the ways they evaluate their own choices.
article.lens: This checkpoint focuses on the tension between internal self-evaluation and the need for external validation. It highlights the shift from studying isolated performance to looking at long-term, autonomous agency and collaborative interaction.
article.title: Tracking How Systems Think About Their Own Reasoning
